doctrine:
**Rules and regulations limiting the substitution of party-list nominees are matters of substance, not form, so they do not lose their mandatory character even after the elections.** The doctrine that election rules are mandatory before the elections but directory after them (Engle v. COMELEC, citing Mitra v. COMELEC) applies only to matters of form. The timing of substitution affects the electorate's right to know who a party-list's nominees are (Lokin; COCOFED; Bantay Republic Act). The COMELEC gravely abuses its discretion when, after the elections and beyond its own deadline, it hastily approves the en masse substitution of all of a winning party-list's nominees. Such approval is void.

Other key rules the Court laid down or reiterated:
- **Section 8 vs. Section 16 of RA 7941.** Section 8 (no change of names or order of nominees after submission, except when a nominee dies, withdraws in writing, or becomes incapacitated; the substitute is placed last) and its implementing COMELEC resolutions govern substitutions before the term starts. Section 16 (a vacancy is filled automatically by the next nominee; additional nominees are submitted once the list is exhausted) applies only to a vacancy in a party-list **seat**, which legally exists only during the term, from noon of June 30 after the election. It does not apply to a vacancy in the list.
- **Withdrawal.** RA 7941 does not prohibit the withdrawal of a nominee, whatever the reason and whether before, during, or after the elections. The COMELEC may neither grant nor deny a withdrawal; it merely notes it.
- **COMELEC rule-making.** Even though RA 7941 sets no deadline for substitution, the COMELEC may validly impose one (Res. No. 9366, as amended by Res. No. 10690) under Section 18 of RA 7941. The deadline is germane to the law's purposes and supplants no express provision, unlike the added ground for withdrawal struck down in Lokin or the statutory deadline moved in PDP-Laban.
- **Administrative function, voting, remedy.** Approving a substitution, and resolving an opposition that needs only the application of laws and rules, is an administrative function. An opposition or a question of fact does not by itself make the proceeding quasi-judicial (Aggabao distinguished). So the COMELEC En Banc may act directly. Article IX-A, Section 7 of the Constitution (majority of all Members) does not apply; a vote of a majority of the Commissioners present at a meeting with a quorum (Sec. 2, COMELEC Res. No. 9936) suffices. Review is by certiorari under Rule 65, not Rule 64.
- **Standing.** Taxpayer, voter, citizen, and legislator suits still require a claim of injury-in-fact. Voters may challenge any rule, regulation, or ruling that injures their rights as voters, not only election laws. Citizens have standing in a case of transcendental importance anchored on the right to information on matters of public concern (Akbayan).
- **TRO and HRET jurisdiction.** The rule that the fallo prevails applies only when it conflicts with the body, not when it merely omits something; an order is read as a whole. A TRO preserves the status quo ante and stays the legal effects of a proclamation and oath, so the nominee does not assume office and jurisdiction stays with the COMELEC, not the HRET.

**Contempt (reiterated).** Indirect contempt is criminal in nature: it requires proof beyond reasonable doubt and contumacious intent, and out-of-court comments on a pending case are punished under the sub judice rule (Rule 71, Sec. 3(d)) only if they pose a clear and present danger to the administration of justice. A person cannot be held in contempt for disobeying an order not addressed to them. A party-initiated charge requires a verified petition (Rule 71, Sec. 4), not a countercharge in a compliance. A lawyer who comments on a pending case to sway public perception, or who spreads false claims on social media, still answers to Canon II of the CPRA (Secs. 19 and 38).
facts:
For the May 9, 2022 elections, COMELEC Resolution No. 10690 (January 27, 2021), amending Resolution No. 9366, required withdrawals of nomination and substitutions due to withdrawal to be filed "not later than NOVEMBER 15, 2021." After that, "NO substitution shall be VALID" unless the original list was exhausted due to death and/or incapacity of the nominees, and such substitutions were allowed only up to mid-day of election day. New lists had to be published within five days of submission. Resolution No. 10717 (August 18, 2021) substantially adopted these rules. Ma. Rowena Amelia V. Guanzon, then a COMELEC Commissioner whose term ended February 2, 2022, signed Resolution No. 10690, and Resolution No. 10717 "also bore Guanzon's imprimatur." P3PWD Party-List filed its petition for registration on March 23, 2021, submitted five nominees on October 6, 2021, and substituted its second to fifth nominees on November 5, 2021 (approved November 24, 2021). Guanzon retired on February 2, 2022, together with Chairperson Abas and Commissioner Kho, leaving four Commissioners.

P3PWD won 391,174 votes (1.0629%), entitling it to one seat. On May 26, 2022, the COMELEC as National Board of Canvassers proclaimed P3PWD and its first nominee, Grace Yeneza, who took her oath on May 30, 2022. Between June 7 and 10, 2022, all five nominees resigned, most citing personal or family reasons. On June 14, 2022, P3PWD filed a board resolution accepting the resignations and a new list of five nominees led by Guanzon (with Rosalie Garcia, Cherrie Belmonte-Lim, Donnabel Tenorio, and Rodolfo Villar, Jr.). The next day, June 15, 2022, the COMELEC En Banc, voting three to one, issued Minute Resolution No. 22-0774. It granted the withdrawals and gave due course to the new list, subject to publication. Commissioner Ferolino concurred on the withdrawals but voted to defer the new list. P3PWD published the list on June 15 and 17, 2022.

On June 17, 2022, Duterte Youth Party-List filed a Verified Opposition. It argued that the substitution came after the deadlines in Resolution No. 9366, as amended, and violated RA 3019 and RA 6713 because Guanzon had just been a member of the COMELEC that approved P3PWD's participation. Without waiting for the Opposition to be resolved, Duterte Youth, through the Cardemas, filed this certiorari petition (G.R. No. 261123) on June 21, 2022. On June 22, 2022, the COMELEC (three approving, Commissioner Ferolino voting to defer) found the publication sufficient (Minute Resolution No. 22-0798) and denied the Opposition (Minute Resolution No. 22-0810). The same day, it proclaimed Guanzon as P3PWD's representative. She took her oath on June 23 before a Court of Appeals Justice and submitted it to the House on June 27, 2022.

On June 29, 2022, the Supreme Court issued a TRO. Its "whereas" portion stated the need to enjoin both the COMELEC from implementing the resolution and the House from allowing Guanzon and the other substitutes to assume office, but its dispositive portion enjoined only the COMELEC. On June 30, 2022, Guanzon filed House Bill No. 440 (later Nos. 1044 and 1868). The House, through the OSG, manifested on July 14, 2022 that it would comply with the TRO out of courtesy and returned her bills. On July 1, 2022, Ronald Cardema also filed with the COMELEC a petition to deny due course to or cancel Guanzon's certificate of nomination for material misrepresentation.

Two contempt matters followed. On July 19, 2022, the Court ordered Guanzon to show cause why she should not be cited for violating the sub judice rule over June 23 and 28, 2022 media interviews. In those interviews she said, among other things, that the case belonged to the HRET and asked "what is there to restrain when I already took my oath of office?" In her Compliance she countercharged the Cardemas and their counsel with contempt. Duterte Youth separately filed G.R. No. 261876, charging Guanzon with indirect contempt for defying the TRO: filing a bill, calling herself "Cong" or "Congresswoman," using "OFFICE OF REPRESENTATIVE ROWENA V. GUANZON," and posting that the TRO was moot. Oral arguments were held on November 14, 2023 and January 23, 2024.
issues: Whether the Duterte Youth Party-List and the Cardemas have legal standing to assail the COMELEC Minute Resolutions.

Whether the COMELEC acted in the exercise of its administrative or its quasi-judicial functions in approving the substitution and denying the Opposition, and whether a petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 is the proper remedy.
Whether the petition was premature for having been filed without awaiting the COMELEC's resolution of the Opposition.
Whether jurisdiction remained with the COMELEC or passed to the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (HRET).
Whether RA 7941 prohibits the withdrawal of party-list nominees, and whether Section 8 or Section 16 of RA 7941 governs a substitution made after the elections but before the term begins.
Whether the COMELEC rules on the deadlines for substitution of party-list nominees remain mandatory after the elections.
Whether the COMELEC may impose deadlines for the substitution of nominees when RA 7941 itself sets none.
Whether the Minute Resolutions are void for not having been approved by at least four Commissioners under Article IX-A, Section 7 of the Constitution.
Whether the COMELEC committed grave abuse of discretion in approving the post-election substitution of all of P3PWD's nominees, and what follows from it.
Whether Guanzon should be held in indirect contempt for violating the sub judice rule.
Whether Guanzon's countercharge for indirect contempt against petitioner, raised in her Compliance, may prosper.
Whether Guanzon is guilty of indirect contempt for violating the June 29, 2022 TRO (G.R. No. 261876).
ruling:
**1. Yes, but only as concerned citizens.** Duterte Youth's claim of an uneven playing field was "too abstract," not the direct injury that standing requires. Its counsel even admitted that it would not lose a seat if P3PWD's nominee sat. Exceptional suits by taxpayers, voters, citizens, and legislators "do not dispense with the requirement that there be a claim of injury-in-fact." The petitioners had no taxpayer standing because no salaries had been paid to the substitutes, and the act assailed did not directly involve the illegal disbursement of public funds; any such injury was "at most indirect and speculative." Ducielle Cardema's interest in seeing that only qualified persons sit in the House "has nothing to do with her prerogatives as a legislator." On voter standing, the Court clarified that the act challenged need not be an election law. It may also be a rule, regulation, or ruling that injures the people's rights as voters. But the petitioners did not even allege that they voted for P3PWD, so they could not have been personally deceived. **Still, given the transcendental importance of the constitutional questions, which involve the people's right to information on matters of public concern in party-list elections, the Cardemas have standing as concerned citizens** (Akbayan Citizens Action v. Aquino).

**2. The COMELEC acted in its administrative capacity, so Rule 64 does not apply, but the petition was treated as one under Rule 65.** The COMELEC's administrative function is the enforcement and administration of election laws, and the En Banc may act on such matters directly. Its quasi-judicial function involves resolving controversies and determining facts on evidence. Under Article IX-C, Section 3, such cases must first be heard in division. Acting on P3PWD's substitution merely enforced laws and rules; receiving a list of substitute nominees is "functionally similar" to receiving COCs and CONAs filed in due form. The Opposition did not change the nature of the proceeding. In *Aggabao*, letters disputing the authenticity of a CONA forced the COMELEC to look beyond its face. Here no conflict of rights arose, and "[a] conflict between an alleged right and a general interest such as the enforcement of laws is not a conflict of rights." **"The existence of an opposition does not automatically convert the proceeding to a quasi-judicial one"** (*Jaramilla*). Questions of fact also do not ipso facto call for quasi-judicial action when the law can simply be applied (*Canicosa*). The COMELEC had only to decide two questions: whether its substitution deadlines were mandatory after the elections, and whether it had jurisdiction over the alleged violations of RA 3019 and RA 6713. Rule 64 excludes administrative rulings, but "the inapplicability of Rule 64 does not foreclose recourse to this Court under Rule 65." In the interest of substantial justice, the Court treated the petition as one under Rule 65.

**3. No, the petition was not premature, because there was no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy.** No COMELEC rule provides a procedure for opposing a substitution; the COMELEC approved it without waiting for any opposition. So filing an Opposition was not a condition sine qua non to certiorari. Motions for reconsideration of en banc rulings are prohibited except in election offense cases (COMELEC Rules, Rule 13, Sec. 1(d)), so Rule 37, Section 1 applies and the ruling may be brought to the Court on certiorari. A petition to deny due course to or cancel a certificate of nomination under Rule 5 of Resolution No. 9366 was not an adequate remedy either: it lies "exclusively on the ground that a material misrepresentation has been committed in the qualification of the nominees." The petition here attacked the substitution as late and as violating RA 3019 and RA 6713.

**4. Jurisdiction remained with the COMELEC because the TRO prevented Guanzon from assuming office.** P3PWD argued that the TRO's dispositive portion restrained only the COMELEC. But the rule that the fallo prevails "speaks of conflict and not mere omission." Where there is no conflict, the fallo is read with the rest of the order (Republic v. De Los Angeles). Otherwise the Court's finding that the House also had to be enjoined would be rendered useless. Guanzon had been proclaimed and had taken her oath, but **the TRO stayed the legal effects of those acts by preserving the status quo ante, the pre-substitution state of affairs.** The Court therefore found it unnecessary to resolve issues on post-substitution acts, such as her proclamation and oath. The House had also manifested that it would comply with the TRO and that Guanzon had not assumed office. Jurisdiction was never acquired by the HRET.

**5. RA 7941 does not prohibit withdrawals, and Section 8, not Section 16, governs.** Section 8 allows a change of names or order of nominees only when a nominee dies, withdraws in writing, or becomes incapacitated (Lokin; COCOFED). It does not prohibit withdrawal itself, so "the COMELEC technically may neither deny nor grant a withdrawal but merely note the same." **"Section 16 applies to a vacancy in a party-list seat, not in the list of nominees."** The seat exists only during the term, which begins at noon of June 30 after the election. This is confirmed by Section 16's command that the next nominee "shall serve for the unexpired term." P3PWD's seat did not legally exist until noon of June 30, 2022, so the mass resignation before then created no vacancy. Section 16's exhaustion clause is a buffer against in-term vacancies; it "was never intended to give party-list groups carte blanche to overhaul the list of nominees." Because the substitution happened before June 30, 2022, Section 8 and its implementing COMELEC resolutions applied.

**6. Yes, the substitution rules remain mandatory after the elections.** P3PWD, Guanzon, and the COMELEC Law Department relied on *Engle v. COMELEC*. But *Engle* itself had qualified the doctrine "to refer only to matters of form" and not to the substantial qualifications of candidates, citing *Mitra v. COMELEC*'s warning against "a blanket and unqualified reading" of it. **"The timing of the substitution of nominees is not merely a matter of form but of substance,"** because it affects the electorate's right to know the nominees and make an informed choice (Lokin; COCOFED; Bantay Republic Act). Treating these rules as directory after the elections would make substitution the rule rather than the exception. Elections would become "a mere sport where players may be substituted at will or on a whim." Any party could also just wait for the elections to end to escape the deadline.

**7. Yes, the COMELEC may impose substitution deadlines even though RA 7941 sets none.** Section 18 of RA 7941 directs the COMELEC to promulgate the rules necessary to carry out the purposes of the Act. The COMELEC may enlarge upon the statute within its standards, so long as its rules are germane to the law's purposes and do not supplant its express provisions. Resolution No. 9366, as amended, merely added a deadline. It did not add a ground for substitution, unlike the rule invalidated in *Lokin*, and it did not move an express statutory deadline, unlike the act struck down in *PDP-Laban*. Without deadlines, the voters' right to make informed choices would be rendered nugatory. The Court noted that it had likewise upheld the COMELEC's publication requirement in *COCOFED* and *Lokin* even though no statute expressly required it. "[N]ot every imposition of a deadline or added requirement not expressly required by statute will be considered a modification or supplantation thereof."

**8. No, the three-to-one vote was valid.** Article IX-A, Section 7 ("majority vote of all its Members") governs only decisions, rulings, and orders issued in the exercise of quasi-judicial powers (Garces v. Court of Appeals). For administrative matters, Section 2 of COMELEC Resolution No. 9936 applies: a decision or resolution is valid when approved by "a majority of all the members of the Commission present at a meeting at which there is a quorum," and a quorum is a majority of the members with existing and valid appointments. **The approval of the substitution and the denial of the Opposition were administrative acts, so three affirmative votes out of four Commissioners were enough.**

**9. Yes, the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion.** P3PWD invoked *Angcos v. Duterte Youth*, a minute resolution that dismissed a challenge to Duterte Youth's own post-2019 substitution. But a minute resolution is res judicata only as to the same subject matter, issues, and parties, and it is not binding precedent for other parties. In *Liberal Party v. COMELEC*, the COMELEC's violation of its own mandatory deadline amounted to grave abuse of discretion. Here, besides clearly disregarding its own deadline, the COMELEC approved the substitution with "sheer speed," one day after P3PWD's physical filing. Undue haste, taken with other circumstances, may show arbitrariness. Commissioner Ferolino's memorandum described those circumstances:
- short shrift to the publication requirement;
- brushing aside the rules for a former Commissioner, when in a previous instance the COMELEC had only noted the substitute nominations;
- pre-approving the new list pending publication; and
- one Commissioner's suggestion that the approval could simply be recalled if publication was not made.

Taken together with the undue haste, these showed grave abuse of discretion: "[T]he COMELEC En Banc shamelessly allowed itself to be used as a tool in perpetuating a scheme." **Minute Resolution No. 22-0774 is void insofar as it approved the substitution.** It remains valid as to the withdrawals, though that approval was unnecessary. P3PWD is not without recourse: the faults of P3PWD and the COMELEC cannot disenfranchise an entire sector, and Section 16 requires the submission of additional nominees once the list is exhausted during the term. But since P3PWD could not legally substitute the five nominees, it cannot renominate them for the Nineteenth Congress, because "what cannot be legally done directly cannot be done indirectly." The Court acknowledged that Section 16 might be used during the term to get around Section 8, but held that only the Legislature can close that gap. The Court added a reminder: a candidate who files for office or a nominee who accepts a nomination enters into a "political contract" with the electorate to assume office and serve if elected.

**10. No contempt was imposed, though Guanzon's remarks were "borderline contumacious."** Violating the sub judice rule is indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(d). Proceedings for indirect contempt are criminal in nature: the respondent is presumed innocent, guilt requires proof beyond reasonable doubt, and intent is material, so good faith is a defense. Because free expression is involved, the "clear and present danger" test applies (Marantan v. Diokno). By commenting on jurisdiction, which goes into the merits, and invoking her standing as a lawyer and law professor, Guanzon seemed to be priming public sentiment, "an improper use of her influence." The Court reminded her of CPRA Canon II, including Section 19, which bars lawyers from using any medium to comment on a pending case in a way that may sway public perception. But contumacious intent was not shown beyond reasonable doubt. She had not yet received a copy of the petition, and her phrase "without meaning to jump the gun on the Supreme Court" showed deference. **There was no clear and present danger; "[i]n borderline instances such as this, freedom of public comment should weigh heavily against a possible tendency to influence pending cases."** The Court warned that its restraint is not tolerance: "Courts, after all, are courts of law and not of public opinion."

**11. No, the countercharge was dismissed.** Under Rule 71, indirect contempt is commenced either by the court motu proprio or by the affected party through a verified petition. For a party-initiated charge, the verified petition is mandatory. It is treated independently of the main case and must meet the requirements for initiatory pleadings, such as a certification against forum shopping and the payment of docket fees. **Guanzon's countercharge, raised in her Compliance instead of a separate petition, was procedurally defective.**

**12. No, Guanzon did not commit contempt by violating the TRO (G.R. No. 261876 dismissed).** **"A party cannot be held in contempt for disobeying a court order which is not addressed to them,"** and the TRO was directed only at the COMELEC and the House. She received the TRO and the petition only on July 4, 2022, so she was unaware of any bar when she filed a bill on June 30, 2022. Her June 29 post that she would reply to the petition did not show knowledge of the TRO. Her later use of "Cong," "Congresswoman," and "OFFICE OF REPRESENTATIVE" might expose her to other liability if proven malicious, but it was not defiance of a TRO not addressed to her. Still, the Court held that by claiming to be a congresswoman while aware that the TRO restrained her substitution, "she disseminated a false claim and committed an act of disinformation," and it reminded her of the CPRA rule on the responsible use of social media (ABS-CBN Corp. v. Ampatuan, Jr.). Her July 15 post calling the TRO moot quoted a news article and merely restated her position in the case, without malice or insult to the Court. The contempt power is exercised "on the preservative and not on the vindictive principle."
disposition:
The Petition in G.R. No. 261123 was GRANTED. COMELEC Minute Resolution No. 22-0774 dated June 15, 2022 was declared NULL and VOID for having been issued with grave abuse of discretion insofar as it approved the substitution of P3PWD's nominees. The TRO dated June 29, 2022 was made PERMANENT. P3PWD was DIRECTED to submit additional nominees under Section 16 of RA 7941 but was STRICTLY ENJOINED from renominating, for the duration of the Nineteenth Congress, Ma. Rowena Amelia V. Guanzon, Rosalie J. Garcia, Cherrie B. Belmonte-Lim, Donnabel C. Tenorio, and Rodolfo B. Villar, Jr.

The Petition for indirect contempt in G.R. No. 261876 was DISMISSED for lack of merit. Guanzon's countercharge for indirect contempt was DISMISSED for being procedurally defective. The Decision was declared immediately executory.

bar_questions.q:
Bayanihan Workers Party-List (BWP) submitted its five nominees to the COMELEC in October 2024. A COMELEC resolution for the May 2025 elections provided that withdrawals and substitutions due to withdrawal must be filed not later than November 15, 2024. After that date, no substitution would be valid unless the original list was exhausted by death or incapacity of the nominees, and then only until mid-day of election day. BWP won one seat, and its first nominee was proclaimed on May 26, 2025. In early June 2025, all five nominees resigned for personal reasons. On June 10, 2025, BWP filed a new list of five nominees led by Atty. Mara. The next day, the COMELEC En Banc approved the substitution by a vote of three of its four sitting Commissioners. Celso, a citizen, filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 65 with the Supreme Court.

(a) BWP argues that election rules are merely directory after the elections, and that Section 16 of RA 7941 allows it to submit new nominees once its list is exhausted. Is the substitution valid?

(b) Celso argues that the COMELEC resolution is void in any case because only three Commissioners approved it, short of the majority of all seven Members required by Article IX-A, Section 7 of the Constitution. Is Celso correct?

alac.answer: (a) No. The substitution is void, and the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion in approving it. (b) No. The three-vote approval is not void on that ground, because approving a substitution is an administrative act.
alac.legal_basis: Rules and regulations limiting the substitution of party-list nominees are matters of substance and do not lose their mandatory character even after the elections. The rule that election rules become directory after the elections applies only to matters of form (Engle v. COMELEC, citing Mitra v. COMELEC). Before the term begins, substitution is governed by Section 8 of RA 7941 and the COMELEC's implementing deadlines, which the COMELEC may validly impose under Section 18 of RA 7941. Section 16 of RA 7941 applies only to a vacancy in a party-list seat, which exists only during the term that begins at noon of June 30 after the election. Violating its own mandatory deadline is grave abuse of discretion on the COMELEC's part (Liberal Party v. COMELEC). Approving a substitution is an administrative function. Article IX-A, Section 7 applies only to decisions issued in the exercise of quasi-judicial powers, so an administrative resolution approved by a majority of the Commissioners present at a meeting with a quorum (Section 2, COMELEC Resolution No. 9936) is valid. (Duterte Youth Party-List v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 261123, August 20, 2024)
alac.application: (a) BWP's substitution came after the elections and long after the November 15, 2024 deadline. Its nominees did not die or become incapacitated; they resigned. Because the timing of substitution affects the voters' right to know the nominees behind the party they voted for, the deadline remains mandatory after the elections. Section 16 does not help BWP. Its seat would legally exist only at noon of June 30, 2025, so the mass resignation in early June created no vacancy in a seat. By approving the substitution in violation of its own mandatory deadline, and only a day after the filing, the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion, and its approval is void. (b) Approving the substitution only applied election laws and rules and did not adjudicate any conflict of rights, so it was administrative. Article IX-A, Section 7 does not apply. Three of the four sitting Commissioners are a majority of those present at a meeting with a quorum, so the vote was enough. The resolution is void only because of its substantive defect, not because of the vote count.
alac.conclusion: The substitution is void for grave abuse of discretion, but not because of the three-to-one vote, which was sufficient for an administrative act.

bar_questions.q:
Kalinga ng Bayan Party-List won one seat in the May 2025 elections. Its first nominee, Dante, assumed office as party-list representative at noon of June 30, 2025. In March 2026, Rep. Dante resigned from the House of Representatives. Over the next two weeks, the party's second to fifth nominees each filed a written withdrawal of nomination, citing only "personal reasons." The party then submitted a list of additional nominees to the COMELEC.

(a) A rival party asks the COMELEC to deny the withdrawals because "personal reasons" is not a valid cause for withdrawal. Should the COMELEC deny them?

(b) The rival also argues that under Duterte Youth Party-List v. COMELEC, a party-list can never replace its nominees after the elections. May the party submit additional nominees?

alac.answer: (a) No. The COMELEC may not deny the withdrawals; it may only note them. (b) Yes. The vacancy arose in an existing seat during the term, so Section 16 of RA 7941 requires the party to submit additional nominees once its list is exhausted.
alac.legal_basis: Section 8 of RA 7941 does not prohibit the withdrawal of nominees, whatever the reason and whether before, during, or after the elections. What it prohibits is a change of names or alteration of the order of nominees after the list is submitted, subject to exceptions. Hence the COMELEC may neither grant nor deny a withdrawal but merely notes it. Section 16 of RA 7941 provides that a vacancy in the seats reserved for party-list representatives is filled automatically by the next nominee, who serves for the unexpired term. If the list is exhausted, the party shall submit additional nominees. Section 16 applies to a vacancy in a seat, which exists only during the term of the party-list representative, not to a vacancy in the list before the term begins. (Duterte Youth Party-List v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 261123, August 20, 2024)
alac.application: (a) The rival assumes that the law limits the grounds for withdrawal. It does not. The nominees' written withdrawals need no approval, and the COMELEC's role is only to note them. (b) In Duterte Youth, the substitution was void because it was made after the elections but before the term began, when no seat legally existed and Section 8 still governed. Here the term began at noon of June 30, 2025, and Rep. Dante's resignation in March 2026 created a vacancy in an existing seat. With the second to fifth nominees gone, there is no next nominee to fill it, so the list is exhausted. Section 16 itself then commands the party to submit additional nominees. The Court in Duterte Youth recognized that Section 16 might be used this way to get around Section 8, but it held that only Congress can close that gap.
alac.conclusion: The COMELEC should only note the withdrawals, and the party may submit additional nominees under Section 16 of RA 7941.

bar_questions.q:
While a petition challenging her substitution as a party-list nominee was pending in the Supreme Court, Atty. Lina, a former law professor, told reporters, before receiving a copy of the petition: "In my humble opinion as a lawyer and law professor, the Supreme Court cannot restrain what is already done. The case belongs to the HRET. Without meaning to jump the gun on the Supreme Court, I have already taken my oath." The Court then issued a TRO addressed only to the COMELEC and the House of Representatives. After receiving a copy of the TRO, Atty. Lina kept calling herself "Congresswoman" on her social media accounts. The petitioner filed a verified petition to cite Atty. Lina for indirect contempt for violating the sub judice rule and for defying the TRO.

(a) Should Atty. Lina be held in indirect contempt?

(b) Is she free of any accountability as a lawyer for her conduct?

alac.answer: (a) No. Her remarks, though borderline, pose no clear and present danger to the administration of justice, and she cannot be held in contempt for disobeying a TRO not addressed to her. (b) No. Her conduct runs against her duties of propriety under Canon II of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA).
alac.legal_basis: Violating the sub judice rule is indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(d) of the Rules of Court. Indirect contempt proceedings are criminal in nature: the respondent is presumed innocent, guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, and intent is material, so good faith is a defense. Comments on a pending case are punished only if they pose a clear and present danger, meaning a serious and imminent threat, to the administration of justice (Marantan v. Diokno; ABS-CBN Corp. v. Ampatuan, Jr.). A party cannot be held in contempt for disobeying a court order not addressed to them. Canon II of the CPRA requires lawyers to maintain the appearance of propriety. Section 19 bars them from using any forum or medium to comment on a pending case in a way that may sway public perception. Section 38 bars them from knowingly or maliciously disseminating false or unverified claims or committing other acts of disinformation on social media. (Duterte Youth Party-List v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 261123, August 20, 2024)
alac.application: (a) Atty. Lina's remarks went into the merits (jurisdiction) and invoked her expertise in a way that could prime public opinion, which is improper. But she spoke before receiving the petition and relied only on news reports, and she expressly deferred to the Court ("without meaning to jump the gun"). These facts negate contumacious intent beyond reasonable doubt, and her words do not seriously and imminently threaten the Court's independence. In borderline cases, freedom of public comment weighs heavily against a possible tendency to influence pending cases. As to the TRO, it enjoined only the COMELEC and the House, so what she did after receiving it was not contempt of that order. (b) Commenting publicly on the merits of a pending case to sway opinion runs against Canon II, Section 19. Calling herself "Congresswoman" on social media while knowing that the TRO restrained her substitution spreads a false claim, an act of disinformation under Canon II, Section 38. If shown to be malicious, it may expose her to liability other than contempt.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Lina should not be held in indirect contempt, but her statements and posts may make her answerable as a lawyer under Canon II of the CPRA.

notes: Consolidated with G.R. No. 261876 (petition for indirect contempt against Guanzon), resolved in the same Decision. Votes: Gesmundo, C.J., Caguioa, Hernando, Zalameda, M. Separate opinions were not used. The Court said it was not bound to pass upon every issue in its Revised Advisory if not indispensable, and it did not resolve these listed issues: whether the substitutes had to comply with Section 9 of RA 7941, whether Guanzon as a former COMELEC Commissioner was an eligible substitute (the RA 3019 and RA 6713 objection), and which oath marks assumption of office for HRET jurisdiction (held unnecessary because the TRO preserved the pre-substitution state).
